<reason>CON built a sharp case around "achievable" and landed real hits: PRO could not name an existing Israeli coalition (only "the same kind" as Gaza's), the Gaza-evacuation trauma scaled up, and PRO's falsifier threshold being undefined. But the motion is comparative ("least-bad"), and PRO correctly forced CON's alternative through the same test. PRO's "same door" argument—that a rights-based single state still ends with a national majority accepting minority status, so any pressure sufficient for that would buy a border more cheaply—was never squarely neutralized. CON's incrementalism answer (A4.1–A4.3) was clever, but PRO's reply that the increments still sum to the majority yielding sovereignty, with Hebron settlers inside the legislature rather than outside it, held, and CON's closing partly conceded that "both roads run through hard Israeli politics." PRO also turned CON's A2 mechanism (collapse of temporariness/formal annexation forcing the world to price it) into a damaging point under "least-bad": a plan that begins by locking in hierarchy and hoping it backfires. CON had two clipped turns and no falsifier for its own trajectory; PRO had one clipped turn and a mislabeled reference id. Close and well-fought, but PRO made the decisive comparison easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's pressure Q1 ("movable or immovable?") followed by B4.6–B4.7 and B5.2: equality is enacted or it isn't, increments sum to a majority dissolving its own state, and whatever pressure could extract that could extract a border far more cheaply. CON's "different-sized asks" answer was the best available response but left the door standing.</best_rebuttal>
